Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I am permanently an outsider now
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Maya Chen sat on the edge of the office chair, her hands folded tightly in her lap, still braced against the weight of the Tuesday she could not name. At thirty-five, she was a working actor whose career had once been built on her ability to inhabit other lives. Now, she felt permanently unmoored from her own. The rupture had begun in a crowded transit concourse, where she had been waiting to transfer to a dry run. Without warning, the space fractured into chaos. Armed officers in dark tactical gear poured into the concourse, rifles raised, uniforms brushing against her shoulders as they herded people against concrete pillars. She could not piece the afternoon together into a coherent account. What remained were disconnected fragments: the stiff wool of a vest, the sharp glint of a trigger guard, the deafening echo of boots on tile. When these images surfaced later, they did not arrive as recollections. They felt like the present moment, pulling her backward with such force that her pulse would hammer against her ribs. What frightened her most was that the fear, horror, or shame would surge so strongly that she was certain that the danger was still unfolding. Even when her manager called to insist the city was quiet, even when her neighbors pointed out the ordinary rhythm of traffic, she found it impossible to trust that the threat had passed. In every new room, her eyes automatically cataloged sightlines and corners. She would arrive at auditions, at cafes, at friend gatherings, and always choose the seat by the wall, the one angled toward the door, the one that felt protected. Alongside this vigilance, she developed another habit. When the pressure built behind her sternum, she would swipe her card for objects she never needed-overpriced vintage mirrors, last-minute concert tickets, stacks of linen she would never unpack. The spending served only to distract herself, leaving her accounts drained and her hands trembling afterward. Over the following months, these patterns settled into her routine. She could not walk past a man in a police uniform without her throat closing. Seeing a prop sidearm mounted on a rehearsal set sent her out of the studio and back into her car. She stopped taking public transport altogether, relying on costly rideshares that ate into her audition fund and forced her to turn down last-minute callbacks. Her casting directors noticed the cancellations. Her friends noticed the missed calls. She had come to believe that the perpetrators of that day had faced no consequences, that justice had simply folded in on itself, and that she was permanently an outsider, watching everyone else live in a world that no longer included her. The isolation felt less like a choice and more like a physical distance, a glass wall that no amount of speaking could breach. Maya came to therapy because the glass had become too heavy to carry. She sought help not for a diagnosis, but for a way to sit in a room without scanning the exits, to remember without feeling it, to stop paying for quiet. What she feared most was that the fragments would keep tearing through her work and her relationships until there was nothing left. What she hoped for was simpler: to believe the room was safe, to trust her own hands, and to finally stop waiting for the noise to end.
